title: CBSE Class 10 English Language and Literature · Practice paper 1
subject: English Language and Literature
label: Practice paper
instr: This question paper contains 24 questions. All questions are compulsory.

The question paper is divided into three sections:
Section A: Reading Skills (20 marks), questions 1 and 2
Section B: Grammar and Creative Writing Skills (20 marks), questions 3 to 14
Section C: Literature (40 marks), questions 15 to 24

The board paper has 11 questions. Here they are numbered so that each task can be answered and marked on its own: questions 3 to 12 are the grammar tasks of board question 3; question 13 is the letter (board question 4); question 14 is the analytical paragraph (board question 5); questions 15 and 16 are the extract-based questions (board questions 6 and 7); questions 17 to 20 are from First Flight (board question 8); questions 21 and 22 are from Footprints without Feet (board question 9); questions 23 and 24 are the long answer questions (board questions 10 and 11).
Answer the short answer questions (17 to 22) in about 40-50 words each, and the letter, the analytical paragraph and the long answer questions (23 and 24) in about 100-120 words each.

Internal choices of the board paper are not included: each question has one version. Where the board paper lets you attempt ten of twelve grammar tasks or four of five short questions, this paper gives only the number you must answer.
Survey figures, names and places in the reading passages and the writing tasks are imaginary and created for practice.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage.

(1) Ask any parent what they dread most during the summer holidays, and many will give the same answer: a child who says, "I'm bored." Within minutes, a screen is switched on, a class is booked or a list of activities appears on the fridge. We treat boredom as a problem to be fixed as quickly as possible. But what if boredom is not an enemy at all? What if it is one of the most useful feelings a young person can have?

(2) Boredom is, at heart, a signal. It tells us that what we are doing no longer holds our attention and that we need something new. Psychologists who study the feeling describe it as uncomfortable but not harmful. Like hunger, it pushes us to act. The real question is what we reach for when it arrives. A child who is handed a phone every time the signal sounds learns only one response: look for something outside yourself to fill the gap.

(3) A child who is allowed to sit with the feeling a little longer often discovers something else. At first there is complaining, then restlessness, and then, surprisingly often, an idea. An old cardboard box becomes a shop counter. A few pebbles turn into a board game with rules invented on the spot. A notebook fills up with a story about a cat who runs a bus company. None of this is planned by an adult, and that is exactly the point.

(4) In one well-known experiment, people who were first given a dull task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, later thought of more creative uses for everyday objects than people who had not been bored. The mind, it seems, wanders when it is under-stimulated, and a wandering mind makes unexpected connections. Daydreaming is not wasted time; it is the brain sorting, linking and imagining.

(5) Boredom also teaches patience and self-reliance. In a world where entertainment is available at the touch of a button, many teenagers find it hard to wait in a queue or sit through a slow chapter of a book. Learning to handle a few empty minutes without panic is a skill, much like learning to swim. It is uncomfortable at first, but it builds a kind of inner strength that lasts.

(6) None of this means that children should be left with nothing to do all day. Hobbies, sport and good books matter. But adults might try a small experiment: the next time a child complains of boredom, resist the urge to rescue. Offer a little time, a little space and perhaps a box of odds and ends. The empty afternoon may turn out to be a gift.

parts.q: (i) In paragraph 1, what does the detail that a screen is switched on 'within minutes' suggest about the way adults respond to a child's boredom?
parts.model: It suggests that adults rush to end a child's boredom at once, treating it as a problem to be fixed instead of letting the child experience it.

points.t: Adults act immediately/hastily to remove boredom, seeing it as a problem to be fixed

parts.q:
(ii) Complete the following with the correct option from the two given.
When the writer compares boredom to hunger (paragraph 2), the point being made is that boredom ________.
(a) is a natural signal that pushes us to do something new
(b) is a harmful feeling that must be satisfied immediately
parts.model: (a) is a natural signal that pushes us to do something new. [The writer says boredom is 'uncomfortable but not harmful' and, like hunger, 'pushes us to act'.]

points.t: Option (a)

parts.q:
(iii) Which of the following is closest to the kind of play described in paragraph 3?
A. A child following step-by-step instructions to build a model kit
B. A child turning old bottle caps into pieces for a game she has made up
C. A child watching a video on how to draw cartoons
D. A child attending a summer art class run by a teacher
parts.model: B. A child turning old bottle caps into pieces for a game she has made up. [Like the pebbles and the cardboard box, the play is invented by the child, not planned by an adult.]

points.t: Option B

parts.q: (iv) Based on paragraph 4, explain how being bored can lead to creative thinking.
parts.model: When the mind is under-stimulated, it begins to wander and daydream. A wandering mind links ideas in unexpected ways, so new ideas appear. This is why the people who had done a dull task later thought of more creative uses for everyday objects.

points.t: Boredom/under-stimulation makes the mind wander or daydream
A wandering mind makes unexpected connections, giving creative ideas (the experiment: more creative uses for everyday objects)

parts.q:
(v) State whether the following statement is True or False. (Paragraph 5)
The writer suggests that the ability to cope with empty time is something children are either born with or without.
parts.model: False. [The writer calls it a skill that is learnt, 'much like learning to swim'.]

points.t: False

parts.q:
(vi) Complete the analogy by selecting the correct option, (a) or (b).
boredom : a signal :: daydreaming : ________
(a) wasted time
(b) the brain sorting and linking ideas
parts.model: (b) the brain sorting and linking ideas. [The passage describes boredom as 'a signal' and daydreaming as 'the brain sorting, linking and imagining'; it says daydreaming is not wasted time.]

points.t: Option (b)

parts.q:
(vii) Read the statements (i)-(v) and select the option that correctly classifies them as Facts (F) or Opinions (O).
(i) In the experiment described, some people were given the task of copying numbers from a telephone directory.
(ii) Boredom is one of the most useful feelings a young person can have.
(iii) The empty afternoon may turn out to be a gift.
(iv) Hobbies, sport and good books matter.
(v) Psychologists study the feeling of boredom.
A. (i) F (ii) F (iii) O (iv) O (v) O
B. (i) O (ii) O (iii) F (iv) F (v) F
C. (i) F (ii) O (iii) O (iv) O (v) F
D. (i) F (ii) O (iii) F (iv) O (v) O
parts.model: C. (i) F (ii) O (iii) O (iv) O (v) F

points.t: Option C

parts.q: (viii) Why does the writer end the passage by suggesting 'a small experiment' to adults instead of laying down a strict rule? (Paragraph 6)
parts.model: The writer wants to persuade gently. Calling it an experiment invites adults to try it and see the results for themselves, which is more convincing than an order. It also keeps the argument balanced: the writer has just accepted that hobbies and activities matter, so the suggestion is a small, practical change, not an extreme one.

points.t: Invites adults to try it and see the results for themselves; gentle persuasion is more convincing than a rule
Keeps a balanced tone: the writer accepts that hobbies/activities matter, so suggests only a small, practical change

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following passage.

(1) Millets such as jowar, bajra and ragi were once everyday food in many Indian homes. Over the decades, polished rice and wheat took their place on most plates. Now millets are making a quiet comeback. The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, and since then schools, restaurants and food companies have begun to promote these hardy grains.

(2) Millets grow well on dry land and need far less water than rice. They are rich in fibre, iron and calcium, and they keep a person feeling full for longer. For farmers in areas with uncertain rainfall, they are a safer crop.

(3) A survey of 400 families in Sundarpur, a small town, asked how often they ate millet dishes in 2022 and again in 2026. The results are given below.
How often the family ate millet dishes20222026
At least once a day6%15%
A few times a week14%31%
Rarely52%40%
Never28%14%


(4) Families who had increased their use of millets gave three main reasons: health advice from doctors (58%), millet dishes served in school meals (27%) and recipes shared on social media (15%). Those who still ate millets rarely said that the grains took longer to cook and that their children preferred the taste of rice and wheat.

(5) Nutrition experts say the trend is encouraging, but they warn that packaged millet snacks loaded with salt and sugar do not offer the same benefits as simple home-cooked meals.

parts.q:
(i) Complete the sentence by selecting the correct option from those given in the bracket.
The phrase 'making a quiet comeback' in paragraph 1 suggests that millets are ________. (suddenly becoming the most popular food / gradually returning to people's diets)
parts.model: gradually returning to people's diets

points.t: gradually returning to people's diets

parts.q: (ii) Why are millets described as a 'safer crop' for farmers in areas with uncertain rainfall? (Paragraph 2)
parts.model: Millets grow well on dry land and need far less water than rice, so the crop is less likely to fail when the rains are poor.

points.t: They grow on dry land/need far less water than rice, so they are less likely to fail when rain is poor

parts.q:
(iii) Select the option that is true for the assertion and reason given below.
Assertion: The share of families who never ate millet dishes halved between 2022 and 2026.
Reason: Millet dishes served in school meals were the most common reason families gave for eating more millets.
A. Both assertion and reason are true, and the reason is the correct explanation.
B. Both are true, but the reason is not the correct explanation.
C. The assertion is true, but the reason is false.
D. The assertion is false, but the reason is true.
parts.model: C. The assertion is true, but the reason is false. [28% fell to 14%, which is half; but health advice from doctors (58%), not school meals (27%), was the most common reason.]

points.t: Option C

parts.q:
(iv) Choose the correct option to complete the sentence.
All of the following are true according to the survey EXCEPT ________.
A. In 2026, almost half of the families ate millet dishes at least a few times a week.
B. The share of families eating millet dishes daily more than doubled.
C. In 2026, a larger share of families ate millet dishes rarely than in 2022.
D. A smaller share of families never ate millet dishes in 2026 than in 2022.
parts.model: C. In 2026, a larger share of families ate millet dishes rarely than in 2022. [The 'rarely' share fell from 52% to 40%. A is true: 15% + 31% = 46%; B is true: 6% rose to 15%; D is true: 28% fell to 14%.]

points.t: Option C

parts.q: (v) Compare the figures for 'Rarely' and 'At least once a day' in 2022 and 2026. What do they suggest about the change in the families' eating habits? (Paragraph 3)
parts.model: The share of families eating millets rarely fell from 52% to 40%, while the share eating them at least once a day rose from 6% to 15%. This suggests that many families have moved from occasional to regular use, so millets are becoming part of everyday meals.

points.t: Correct comparison: 'rarely' fell from 52% to 40%; 'at least once a day' rose from 6% to 15%
Inference: families are moving from occasional to regular use; millets are becoming part of everyday meals

parts.q:
(vi) Complete the sentence suitably. (Paragraph 4)
The main reason why more families in Sundarpur began eating millets was ________.
parts.model: health advice from their doctors (given by 58% of these families)

points.t: health advice from doctors

parts.q: (vii) Identify the word from paragraph 1 that means 'tough and able to survive difficult conditions'.
parts.model: hardy

points.t: hardy

parts.q: (viii) A parent says, "I buy packaged millet chips for my son every day, so he is eating healthily." Based on paragraph 5, how would a nutrition expert respond?
parts.model: The expert would say that packaged millet snacks are often loaded with salt and sugar and do not give the same benefits as simple home-cooked millet meals, so the parent should cook millet dishes at home instead.

points.t: Packaged millet snacks are loaded with salt/sugar and lack the benefits of simple home-cooked millet meals

parts.q: (ix) Suggest one reason why 'Millets: An Old Grain Returns' is a suitable title for the passage.
parts.model: It sums up the passage: millets were traditional everyday food, were replaced by rice and wheat, and are now coming back, as the survey shows (daily use rose from 6% to 15%).

points.t: Links the title to the content: a traditional grain, once replaced, now coming back (supported by the survey)

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the correct option to complete the line from a travel diary.
When we reached the platform at 7:10, our train ________ already, so we had to wait for the next one.
questions.sol: The past perfect 'had left' shows an action completed before another past action (reaching the platform); 'already' supports it.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Report the coach's instruction to the players.
Coach: "Warm up properly before you start running."
questions.model: The coach instructed/advised/told the players to warm up properly before they started running.

points.t: Correct reported form: The coach instructed/told/advised the players to warm up properly before they started (or start) running

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank.
Don't worry, there are still ________ seats left for the evening show; you can book them after lunch.
questions.sol: 'A few' (some) is used with countable nouns and has a positive sense, which fits 'Don't worry'. 'Few' means hardly any; 'little' and 'much' are used with uncountable nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Identify the error in the given line from a news report and supply the correction.
The quality of the mangoes sold in these markets have improved this year.
Use the format: Error | Correction

points.t: Error: have; Correction: has (the subject is 'quality', which is singular)

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the correct option to complete the notice from the school library.
Members ________ return borrowed books within fourteen days; a fine is charged after that.
questions.sol: 'Must' expresses a rule or obligation, which is what a library notice states.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Riya asked her brother, "Where did you keep my geometry box?"
Report Riya's question by completing the sentence.
Riya asked her brother ________.
questions.model: Riya asked her brother where he had kept her geometry box.

points.t: where he had kept her geometry box

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
The given sentence has an error. Select the option that correctly identifies the error and the correction.
She has less friends in her new school than she had in her old one.
questions.sol: 'Friends' is a countable plural noun, so 'fewer' is correct; 'less' is used with uncountable nouns.

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Fill in the blank with the correct form of the verb given in the bracket.
By the time she retired in 2019, my grandmother ________ (teach) in the village school for thirty years.
questions.model: had taught (also accept: had been teaching)

points.t: had taught / had been teaching

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Fill in the blank by choosing the correct option from those given in the bracket.
You ________ carry an umbrella today; the forecast says it will be sunny all day. (needn't / mustn't)

points.t: needn't

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Select the option that correctly reports what Meera said.
Meera said, "I am preparing for the debate tomorrow."
options: Meera said that she is preparing for the debate tomorrow.
Meera told that she was preparing for the debate the next day.
Meera said that she was preparing for the debate the next day.
Meera said that she had prepared for the debate the next day.
questions.sol: The present continuous changes to the past continuous ('was preparing') and 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day'. 'Told' needs an object, and 'had prepared' changes the meaning.

questions.subject: English
questions.text: You are Kavya Menon, 22 Shanti Nagar, Bhopal. Many students of your locality walk to school along Station Road, where the footpaths are broken and are occupied by vendors and parked vehicles. Write a letter in about 120 words to the Editor of a local daily, drawing attention to the danger this causes to pedestrians, especially schoolchildren, and suggesting what the authorities should do.
questions.model:
22 Shanti Nagar
Bhopal
11 January 2027

The Editor
The Bhopal Herald
Bhopal

Subject: Unsafe footpaths on Station Road

Sir/Madam

Through the columns of your esteemed newspaper, I wish to draw the attention of the authorities to the poor condition of the footpaths on Station Road.

Hundreds of schoolchildren walk along this road every morning. However, the footpaths are broken in many places and are occupied by vendors and parked two-wheelers. As a result, children are forced to walk on the road among speeding buses and cars. Two students were injured in minor accidents last month.

I request the Municipal Corporation to repair the footpaths, remove the encroachments and post traffic police near the schools during school hours. Zebra crossings and speed breakers would also help.

I hope the authorities will act before a serious accident occurs.

Yours faithfully
Kavya Menon

points.t: Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, complimentary close and name, all in the correct places
Content: the problem is described (broken, encroached footpaths; children forced onto the road; risk of accidents)
Content: at least two suitable steps are suggested (repairs, removing encroachments, traffic police, zebra crossings or speed breakers)
Organisation: ideas in logical paragraphs (purpose, problem, suggestions, closing appeal) joined with suitable linkers
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct and the tone is formal

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
The table shows how the students of Sunrise Public School travelled to school in 2022 and in 2026. Write an analytical paragraph in about 120 words analysing the changes.
Mode of travel20222026
Walking30%22%
Bicycle12%20%
School bus25%30%
Private car18%10%
Two-wheeler with a parent15%18%
questions.model: The table compares how the students of Sunrise Public School travelled to school in 2022 and 2026. In 2022, walking was the most common mode, at 30%, but by 2026 it had fallen to 22%. The most striking change is the rise in cycling, which went up from 12% to 20%. The school bus also became more popular, rising from 25% to 30%, and was the most common mode in 2026. In contrast, the share of students coming by private car nearly halved, falling from 18% to 10%. Meanwhile, travel on two-wheelers with a parent rose slightly, from 15% to 18%. Overall, the data shows a clear shift towards shared and greener transport, although the fall in walking deserves attention.

points.t: Content: the key changes are reported with correct figures (e.g. cycling 12% to 20%, car 18% to 10%, bus 25% to 30%, walking 30% to 22%)
Content: an overall trend or conclusion is drawn (e.g. a shift towards shared/greener transport), not just a list of figures
Organisation: an introductory sentence and a concluding statement; no title
Organisation: points in a logical order, linked with words of comparison (in contrast, meanwhile, overall)
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Answer the following questions with reference to the context.

Recall the moment in the story when the storm has passed. Lencho stands in the middle of his field with his sons. The hail has destroyed the corn, stripped the leaves from the trees and taken the flowers from the plants, and Lencho says that even a plague of locusts would have left more than the hail has.
(A Letter to God, G. L. Fuentes)

parts.q:
(i) Complete the sentence suitably.
Lencho compares the hail with a plague of locusts to show that ________.
parts.model: the hail has done even more damage than locusts would have done; the crop is totally destroyed and nothing is left

points.t: the damage is total / worse than a plague of locusts; nothing is left

parts.q:
(ii) Which of the following best describes Lencho's state of mind at this moment?
A. angry with his sons for not saving the crop
B. deeply sad and worried about the year ahead
C. calm, as he knows the next harvest will be better
D. relieved that the storm has finally passed
parts.model: B. deeply sad and worried about the year ahead

points.t: Option B

parts.q:
(iii) Fill in the blank with the correct option from the bracket.
Even after this loss, Lencho does not lose hope, because he has firm ________ in God. (faith / doubt)
parts.model: faith

points.t: faith

parts.q: (iv) How does this moment lead to the main action of the story?
parts.model: The total loss leaves the family with nothing and no one to help them. Because Lencho has firm faith in God, this crisis makes him write a letter to God asking for help. The letter then brings in the postmaster's kindness, so the storm is the turning point that tests Lencho's faith and starts the rest of the story.

points.t: The total loss/crisis, with no one to help, makes Lencho turn to God and write a letter asking for help
It is the turning point: it tests his faith and leads to the postmaster's act of kindness

questions.subject: English
questions.text:
Read the following extract and answer the questions that follow.

He stalks in his vivid stripes
The few steps of his cage,
On pads of velvet quiet,
In his quiet rage.
(A Tiger in the Zoo, Leslie Norris)

parts.q:
(i) Complete the sentence suitably.
The phrase 'the few steps of his cage' emphasises the ________ of the tiger's living space.
parts.model: smallness / narrowness (how cramped and limited it is)

points.t: smallness / limited size / confinement

parts.q:
(ii) The word 'stalks' suggests that the tiger moves ________.
A. playfully and fast
B. slowly and quietly, with a sense of threat
C. clumsily and noisily
D. lazily and without purpose
parts.model: B. slowly and quietly, with a sense of threat

points.t: Option B

parts.q:
(iii) Fill in the blank with the correct option from the bracket.
The phrase 'quiet rage' is an example of ________, because it joins two ideas that seem opposite. (oxymoron / simile)
parts.model: oxymoron

points.t: oxymoron

parts.q: (iv) How does the poet use the contrast between the tiger's 'vivid stripes' and his small cage to show his feelings about keeping wild animals in zoos?
parts.model: The 'vivid stripes' suggest the tiger's beauty, strength and wild energy, yet he can walk only 'the few steps of his cage'. The contrast shows that his power is wasted and that he is angry but helpless. Through it the poet expresses sympathy for the tiger and suggests that wild animals belong in their natural home, not in cages.

points.t: Vivid stripes (beauty, power, wildness) set against the few steps of the cage: power wasted, silent anger
The poet's view: sympathy for the tiger; wild animals belong in the wild, not in cages

questions.subject: English
questions.text: What did Nelson Mandela learn about courage from the men and women who struggled against apartheid? How can this idea help a student in a difficult situation? (Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom)
questions.model: Mandela saw his comrades risk and give their lives for an idea. From them he learnt that courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it: the brave man is one who conquers fear. A student who is nervous before a speech can likewise show courage by facing that fear.

points.t: Content: courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it / the brave man conquers fear (learnt from comrades who risked their lives)
Content: a relevant application to a student's situation (feeling afraid but facing the fear)
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: How did Anne Frank turn Mr Keesing's punishment into a chance to show her wit? (From the Diary of Anne Frank)
questions.model: When Mr Keesing set her an essay on 'A Chatterbox', Anne argued that talking is a student's trait, inherited from her mother, who talked as much as she did. After a second essay, he set 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'. With her friend Sanne's help she wrote it as a funny poem. Mr Keesing took the joke well and let her talk in class.

points.t: Content: the essays she argued cleverly (talking is a student's trait, inherited from her mother)
Content: the poem for 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox' won Mr Keesing over; he took the joke well and let her talk
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Why did the pilot take the risk of flying into the storm, and what makes the ending of the story mysterious? (Two Stories about Flying: The Black Aeroplane)
questions.model: Storm clouds stood ahead like black mountains; he could not fly over them and had too little fuel to go round. He could have returned to Paris, but he wanted to get home for breakfast with his family. The ending is mysterious because the woman in the control centre says no other aeroplane was flying that night, so who was the black aeroplane's pilot?

points.t: Content: the risk: could not fly over the clouds, too little fuel to go round; chose not to return to Paris because he wanted to get home (family, breakfast)
Content: the mystery: the woman says no other aeroplane was flying and only his was on the radar, so the helper's identity is unknown
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Why does the poet not offer the boy money to buy another ball? What does the boy learn from his loss? (The Ball Poem, John Berryman)
questions.model: The poet feels that a dime or another ball would be worthless, as the boy must learn to face loss by himself. He learns the 'epistemology of loss': things we own can be lost for ever, money cannot buy them back, and one must accept the loss and stand up again.

points.t: Content: another ball would be worthless; the boy must learn to cope with loss on his own
Content: the lesson: possessions can be lost for ever, money cannot replace them, and one must accept loss and move on
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: How did Mrs Pumphrey's love harm Tricki, and how did Herriot cure him? (A Triumph of Surgery)
questions.model: Mrs Pumphrey overfed Tricki with cream cakes, chocolates, malt, cod-liver oil and Horlicks, and he hardly exercised. He became hugely fat and listless, and later refused food and had bouts of vomiting. Herriot took him to his surgery, gave him no food for two days, only water, and let him run and play with the other dogs. Tricki soon became lively and fit again.

points.t: Content: the harm: overfeeding and no exercise made Tricki fat, listless and ill
Content: the cure: kept at the surgery, no food for two days (only water), exercise and play with other dogs
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: What role did Richard Ebright's mother play in his growth as a scientist? (The Making of a Scientist)
questions.model: His mother encouraged his interest in learning. She took him on trips and bought him telescopes, microscopes, cameras and other equipment, and after his father's death they spent almost every evening learning together. She got him the book 'The Travels of Monarch X', which opened the world of science to him, and wrote to Dr Urquhart so that he could tag monarch butterflies.

points.t: Content: she encouraged his interest in learning: trips, telescopes, microscopes and cameras; evenings of learning together
Content: she got him 'The Travels of Monarch X', which opened the world of science to him, and wrote to Dr Urquhart so he could tag monarchs
Expression: the answer is clear, connected and in about 40-50 words (deduct up to 1 mark overall for grammar or spelling errors)

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Valli's bus ride is both an adventure and a lesson. Discuss how her careful planning shows her independence, and what the sight of the dead cow on her return journey teaches her. (Madam Rides the Bus)
questions.model: Valli, an eight-year-old girl, longed to ride the bus that passed her village. She planned the trip carefully: she found out the fare and the journey time, and saved every coin she got, refusing peppermints, toys and a merry-go-round ride, until she had sixty paise. She slipped away alone during her mother's afternoon nap. On the bus she refused help, paid her own fare and behaved like a grown-up, showing independence and self-respect. The ride was a joyful adventure until, on the way back, she saw the young cow that had earlier run in front of the bus lying dead by the road. The sight showed her that death is real and sudden, and her joy turned to sadness. She returned a little wiser.

points.t: Content: careful planning: finding out the fare and time, saving coins, giving up treats
Content: independence: travels alone, refuses help, pays her own fare, behaves like a grown-up
Content: the dead cow: her first close view of death; joy turns to sadness and she learns that life is uncertain
Expression: ideas are organised logically, with an opening and a conclusion
Expression: the answer is fluent, relevant and in about 100-120 words
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct

questions.subject: English
questions.text: Apprentice Noodle is a minor character, yet he plays an important part in the play. Discuss how Noodle deals with Think-Tank's mistakes and what finally happens to him. (The Book That Saved the Earth)
questions.model: Noodle is the apprentice of Think-Tank, the arrogant ruler of Mars who believes he is never wrong. Noodle always flatters him, calling him 'Great and Mighty Think-Tank' and 'your Cleverness', yet he quietly corrects his mistakes. When Think-Tank says the books are sandwiches to be eaten, Noodle mentions an 'insignificant bit of data': Earthlings did not eat them but used them to communicate. Later he recalls that they opened the books and watched them, and he reminds Think-Tank about the vitamins that increase intelligence. Each time, Think-Tank takes the idea as his own. Noodle's tact keeps him safe while he guides the action. In the end, Think-Tank flees in panic, and the Historian tells us that he was replaced by the wise and wonderful Noodle.

points.t: Content: Noodle flatters Think-Tank ('Great and Mighty', 'your Cleverness') and never contradicts him openly
Content: he corrects mistakes tactfully (books not eaten but used to communicate; opened and watched; vitamins); Think-Tank takes the credit
Content: outcome: Think-Tank flees in panic and is later replaced by 'the wise and wonderful Noodle'
Expression: ideas are organised logically, with an opening and a conclusion
Expression: the answer is fluent, relevant and in about 100-120 words
Accuracy: grammar, spelling and punctuation are correct
